summary.title: Writing a Tiny x86 Bootloader
summary.one_liner: You learn how the BIOS loads a 512-byte boot sector and how to write a small NASM real-mode bootloader that clears the screen, moves the cursor, and prints a string.
keywords: write to usb drive with dd
takeaways: The BIOS loads the first 512 bytes of a bootable medium to 0x7C00 if they end in the 0x55AA signature, then jumps there.
Real mode uses segment:offset addressing (physical = segment*0x10 + offset), so segment registers such as DS and SS must be set via a general register.
BIOS interrupts such as 0x10 provide screen clearing, cursor positioning, and character printing in real mode.
Subroutines follow a stack-based calling convention using push, call, and bp-relative argument access.
The code can be assembled with nasm -f bin, tested in Bochs, or written to a USB drive with dd.
summary.summary:
The author walks through the boot process on an x86 PC, from the BIOS locating a boot sector to the code running at 0x7C00 in 16-bit real mode. The post then builds a minimal NASM bootloader step by step: setting up a stack, then writing subroutines for clearing the screen, moving the cursor, and printing a null-terminated string using BIOS video interrupts. It finishes with the padding and boot signature needed for a 512-byte sector, how to test in the Bochs emulator, and how to write the image to a USB drive with dd.</summary>
